BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: There is solid agreement amongst ensemble members that the active weather pattern will continue through Tuesday, before a warming and drying trend takes hold for the Wednesday into Friday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Next round of precipitation with limited accumulations passes late tonight into early Monday.
- A generally unsettled and wet pattern will continue through next week, with brief dry periods.
- Late week unsettled weather will come alongside warmer temps, with uncertainty on position and inversion development.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Cool and dry conditions continue with broken cloud cover with a ridge overhead. Cloud cover will increase tonight as a surface low and upper shortwave circle around a broader upper low. Precipitation out of the shortwave will favor higher terrain in southeast Oregon and in central Idaho. Snow will begin in eastern Oregon late this evening, with a weak frontal passage moving through southwest Idaho on Sunday and Monday. Minimal accumulations are anticipated with this frontal passage, but colder air at higher elevations in the West Central/Boise Mountains will allow for accumulations between 1-3 inches by Monday morning. Rain will be the predominant precipitation type in the Snake Plain, with a low chance of a brief rain-snow mix on Monday morning. Raw guidance continues to trend much warmer in the mornings than model blends, which lately has indicated a higher chance for precip falling as rain. High pressure will build back in late Monday through Tuesday, bringing a return to dry conditions, with a slight warming trend.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: There is solid agreement amongst ensemble members that the active weather pattern will continue through Tuesday, before a warming and drying trend takes hold for the Wednesday into Friday. This trend isn't fully backed up by deterministic runs, with the GFS and ECMWF along with ECMWF-AIFS showing more of a moist flat ridge pattern setting up Wednesday into the weekend. These differences are introducing a significant amount of uncertainty into the forecast for the latter end of next week. Both scenarios do point to some warming for the area, with snow levels creeping upward to 5000-6000 feet by Friday. This would ensure that most valley locations would remain snow free, with accumulations for the higher mountain valleys and peaks. A wrinkle that could influence where valleys end up is how strong of an inversion sets up under the ridging for the late week. A stronger ridge scenario would help to trap cold air into valleys, including the Long Valley near McCall, which could lower the snow level to valley floor there, even though the upper level pattern would support the higher snow levels mentioned earlier. This could impact holiday travel in and through the mountains. Model trends have been leaning toward the wetter solutions of a flat ridge scenario, with longer rain views showing a return to a series of troughs by early the following week. Needless to say, stay tuned, especially if you have holiday travel plans this week.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: The back edge of the trough will move east of Colorado Tuesday afternoon. Most ensemble members are showing ridging generally over Colorado and the Southwest US starting Wednesday and lasting through the weekend.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Snow showers mainly over the southern foothills and Morgan and eastern Weld Counties ending this afternoon.
- Another system brings the chance for light mountain snow showers late Monday.
- Cooler fall temperatures to continue through mid next week.
- No major travel impacts are expected during the Thanksgiving travel period.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Water vapor imagery shows a trough over Colorado with a strong upper level jet across the eastern half of the state. This jet and PVA from the trough are providing forcing for what has turned into a decent snow event for the foothills and western suburbs of the Denver metro. There were some reports of 3-5" of snow in the foothills with up to 2" in the western metro. This jet is still producing snow showers mainly in two areas. One area is in Morgan and eastern Weld Counties where the best low level frontogenesis in occurring. With the little bit of added elevation in northeastern Weld County, some snow accumulation may have occurred and may continue this afternoon. The other area of snow is mainly across the southern foothills and South Park. It's possible some areas near Westcreek receive 1-3" of snow from the snow showers this afternoon mainly on grassy surfaces. PoPs were increased for both of those areas this afternoon. In the Denver metro, there appears to be too much dry air for any snow showers to form this afternoon. Otherwise, there will be isolated convective snow showers this afternoon over the higher terrain as some instability builds in.

Tonight, skies will clear as the trough moves past Colorado. Light northeast winds will advect moisture from the Northern Plains into Colorado. There may be some patchy fog that develops and with temperatures below freezing, it could create some slick spots on the roadways.
On Sunday, weak ridging will be overhead which will keep conditions dry. Temperatures will remain cool with high clouds and generally light winds.

On Monday, a shortwave trough will move over Colorado. The main PVA forcing from this trough will be split around Colorado with a wave over New Mexico and another in Montana. Lee cyclogenesis will develop across northeast Colorado which will attempt to bring in moisture but there will remain very limited moisture with this system. Due to the weak forcing and limited moisture, the plains are expected to remain dry. The I-70 corridor mountains, Park County, and the southern foothills will have enough instability that develops that snow showers will likely (70% chance) form. Despite the high chance of snow, the snow amounts will be minimal. Generally less than 2" of snow is expected in the mountains with light impacts.

The back edge of the trough will move east of Colorado Tuesday afternoon. Most ensemble members are showing ridging generally over Colorado and the Southwest US starting Wednesday and lasting through the weekend. However, a few (roughly 10-20%) have a trough moving close to Colorado out of northwest flow that could produce light precipitation mainly in the mountains of Colorado Thursday into Friday. Therefore, the forecast calls for a dry Thanksgiving in Denver and across the plains with a chance of light snow in the mountains. Overall, no major travel impacts are expected for the Thanksgiving travel period.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Split flow continues to dominate the long term forecast starting Monday night. An upper level ridge wil be placed over us filtering down the colder air that was displaced from the Arctic.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Scattered snow showers are expected to persist Saturday afternoon and evening, mainly over Carbon County and areas along and north of the US-20 Corridor.
- Chilly temperatures will continue through Tuesday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Not too many changes made to the previous forecast package this afternoon, with a few minor forecast challenges over the next 48 to 60 hours. For this afternoon, current observations and surface analysis shows a stationary cold front across central Wyoming, extending southeast towards the Nebraska/Wyoming border. Occasional snow showers are developing near this front and are slowly moving east into the high plains with some snow accumulation on grassy surfaces observed between Douglas and Casper across far western Converse County. Still dealing with a pretty dry boundary layer this afternoon, especially further south near the I-80 corridor. Kept scattered snow showers in the forecast for mainly east central Wyoming and the higher mountains of southeast Wyoming. Might see a quick inch or two of snow accumulation for the mountains, but maybe a half inch or so for the lower elevations due to the relatively dry airmass. Thankfully, the road temperatures should be warm enough to melt off any snow. However, after sunset...will have to watch some of these heavier snow showers across Niobrara County and the northern Nebraska Panhandle. Can't rule out a few snow squalls as we head into this evening, but winds may be the limiting factor in this case with gusts generally below 35 MPH. Locally slick and icy conditions are possible along and north of highway 20 as snow melts initiatially and then refreezes.

Our coldest night so far this season possible tonight with low temperatures in the teens to low 20s, and some single digits over the more sheltered higher valleys. High resolution guidance shows a reasonable chance (20%-40%) of freezing fog over far southeast Wyoming and the southern Nebraska Panhandle late tonight and into early Sunday morning. This makes sense with models showing winds become light or calm late tonight before switching into the south just prior to sunrise. Although not totally confident with fog development, added patchy freezing fog to Pine Bluffs, Kimball, and Sidney Nebraska since models have been underestimating this potential in recent weeks. Not expecting dense fog at this time with probabilities of one half mile or less visibility currently around 10%. Some fog may also develop along the lower North Platte River Valley, but probabilities are far less compared to the southern panhandle. Chilly day on Sunday with highs in the mid to upper 30s for most of southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska.

For Monday, models indicate a transient shortwave ridge axis translating eastward over the region in the morning as the next poorly organized upper level trough moves into the eastern Great Basin Region. Mainly dry conditions are expected with some snow showers developing over the mountains later on Monday. Below average temperatures will continue with highs struggling to reach 40 degrees for most locations under mostly cloudy skies.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Split flow continues to dominate the long term forecast starting Monday night. An upper level ridge wil be placed over us filtering down the colder air that was displaced from the Arctic. A weak shortwave will also push through the region Monday night but unless you're on top of the Sierra madres and possibly adjacent valley's, I wouldn't get my hopes up about seeing snow any time soon. The global models (GFS,EURO,and Canadian) all seem too progressive with this ridge breaking down enough to let another system push into the Pacific NW and potentially giving us some chances for snow for the lower elevations. However, typically in a split flow regime the intermountain west usually gets nothing when we are smack dab in the middle of it. THe lobes of vorticity are co- located with the low pressure systems with almost no synoptic forcing over us to create precipitation with the exception of our mountain peaks. However, under the ridge the cold airmass will undergo some modification and 700mb temperatures will have a slight increase from -3 degree to a positive 3 degrees which means areas along and east of I-25 may expect to have temperatures reach into the 50's come Thanksgiving day and every shopper's coveted "holiday" known as black friday.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: There continues to be a vague signal of another system passing through late next week, but models are not in good agreement. Some solutions depict wet weather, while others not so much.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Generally dry and cooler conditions for the majority of the weekend.
- Most desert valleys will likely see their first taste of below freezing overnight lows this weekend.
- Active weather remains possible for Thanksgiving week, but some details still remain uncertain. Stay tuned for updates to timing and impacts as they become available.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Light snow will continue to make its way out of the forecast area by this afternoon as the trough axis swings through. Local cameras in the San Juans appear to show a few inches of snow fell overnight, with snow still falling in some locations. Generally, as the cloud cover begins to burn off this morning, most locations will see sunny skies and decreased precipitation chances. Otherwise, temperatures have notably dropped behind the frontal boundary which passed through yesterday. This means that overnight lows for the next several nights are tracking to drop below freezing for a large swath of the area. Any valley locations which have yet to hit freezing will likely be hitting it sometime this weekend.

A low-amplitude ridge builds in behind the exiting trough Saturday evening into Sunday morning. This means that Sunday's weather will be relatively similar to Saturday. One point of note would be there is a possibility for clearing skies overnight into Sunday morning which could support localized fog in some valleys. The current forecast isn't overly bullish about this factor though, so there remains uncertainty. By Sunday evening, upper-level flow turns back to southwesterly ahead of an approaching trough. Moisture and forcing appear unimpressive with this system, so current expectations are for only light showers Sunday evening through Tuesday morning. Snow accumulations are on track to sit below advisory level.

There continues to be a vague signal of another system passing through late next week, but models are not in good agreement. Some solutions depict wet weather, while others not so much. Therefore, this far out, that forecast should be taken with a grain of salt. This potential storm could impact Thanksgiving travel, so stay tuned for additional updates to the forecast as those dates approach, especially if you plan on traveling for the holiday.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Models continue to diverge for further into the Thanksgiving Holiday week, with the GFS camp digging a system south across the Desert SW and into Old Mexico through Friday, with the EC and Canadian keeping another weak trough translating across the Northern Rockies later Wednesday, with moderate northwest flow aloft across the region on Thanksgiving Day into next Friday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Drier air behind passing system to bring quick clearing this evening and cool overnight lows.
- Dry with continued below seasonal temperatures Sunday.
- Another quick moving system bringing light mountain snows and passing showers to the plains Monday into Monday night.
- Another system possible late week with mountain snows possible though model/ensemble consensus is trending drier for the plains.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Current water vapor imagery and upper air analysis has an upper trough digging across the Rockies this morning, with a rather sharp baroclinic zone translating across the central Colorado at this time. Current webcams cams have snow covered roads across the Wolf Creek and Monarch Passes, along with some snow falling near Buena Vista and Wilkerson Pass at this time.

Clouds and precipitation associated with the passing front will continue to lift out across the Front Range through the early afternoon and continue across the plains into the early evening, with some light snow expected across the higher terrain of Rampart Range and the southeast mtns, with potential accumulations of a few inches. Best chances of seeing some light snowfall on grassy areas across the plains remains along the Palmer Dvd and Pikes Peak region, where low level upslope will help moisten the atmosphere. We do not anticipate any travel issues with roads remaining warm.

A cooler, drier and subsident airmass moves in behind the parting system tonight, leading to clearing skies and cool overnight lows mainly in the 20s across the plains, and in single digits and teens across the higher terrain.

Modest west to northwest flow across the region tomorrow will keep dry conditions in place, with slowly increasing mid and upper level moisture moving across the region through the day. Temperatures look to remain below seasonal levels in the 40s across the plains and in the 30s and 40s across the higher terrain, save for 20s at the peaks.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Another quick moving system remains progged to dig across the Great Basin Sunday night and continue across western Colorado through the day Monday and across eastern Colorado Monday night. This system looks similar to today's system, as there is not a lot of available moisture associated with it, and looks to bring another quick shot of light snow to mountains, with possible accumulations of 1 to 3 inches across the ContDvd, and another few inches possible across the rest of the higher terrain, along with a few passing snow showers across the plains. Temperatures remain cool behind this system on Tuesday, with dry conditions expected.

Models continue to diverge for further into the Thanksgiving Holiday week, with the GFS camp digging a system south across the Desert SW and into Old Mexico through Friday, with the EC and Canadian keeping another weak trough translating across the Northern Rockies later Wednesday, with moderate northwest flow aloft across the region on Thanksgiving Day into next Friday. Latest NBM data seemingly splits model solutions keeping pops along the Continental Divide for Thursday into Friday, with the plains dry. Highs look to warm back into the 50s across the plains, with 30s and 40s across the higher terrain for Thursday and Friday. Time will tell.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Longwave ridging is forecast to build across the region for the middle to latter portion of the week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A cool and stable airmass will settle across the region through the weekend.
- A weak weather system will bring a chance of snow showers mainly to northern Utah Monday, with little if any accumulation.
- Another weak system is forecast to cross the region on Thanksgiving. This will bring a small chance for valley rain and mountain snow to northern Utah, while southern Utah remains largely dry.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Shortwave ridging building into the Great Basin will bring large scale subsidence across the forecast area through the remainder of the day. Lingering show showers continue to wane late this morning, and will end by early afternoon as this upstream ridge continues to build east. As such, aLlowed the remaining winter wx headlines to expire as scheduled. With temperatures. A cool and increasingly stable airmass settling in across the forecast area will keep daytime temperatures several degrees below normal for the latter portion of November. Temperatures tonight will trend a few degrees warmer across southern Utah, and will remain above freezing across lower Washington County, thus no additional freeze products are anticipated.

The upstream shortwave ridge will move east on Sunday allowing southwesterly flow to overspread the forecast area in advance of an approaching shortwave trough. The resultant warming trend will push daytime temperatures back near climo Sunday. This progressive, moisture starved trough quickly translate across the region Monday, bringing a chance for mainly mountain showers with minimal accumulation.

Longwave ridging is forecast to build across the region for the middle to latter portion of the week. A splitting shortwave trough fighting its way through this mean ridge position is forecast to translate through the Great Basin region late Wednesday into early Thanksgiving Day. Given the splitting nature of this wave, forcing/moisture will remain limited, and like the early week system, the chance for precipitation is low (20-30%) and largely confined to northern Utah.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: You could trigger an avalanche large enough to bury you from a distance, from below, or on steep leeward slopes below ridgelines and around rocky convexities. The most dangerous slopes are north and northeast-facing slopes above treeline.

Strong winds preceded Friday night's snowfall, meaning that stiff wind-drifted slabs are now hidden under a blanket of low-density snow. With visual surface clues hidden, rely on good terrain selection and travel techniques to avoid triggering a dangerous avalanche. Safer travel can be found in wind-sheltered areas below treeline.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: There isn't enough snow for avalanches on most slopes. Steer around hard drifts of snow on steep terrain features and below ridgetop in the alpine.

3046.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has begun to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. 6-12 inches of new snow has fallen between Friday the 13th and Monday the 16th. Another 6-12 inches could stack up by the end of the week. If you're traveling in the mountains this week, watch out for wind slabs 1-2 feet thick above 7,000 feet and pay attention to terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: From 60-degree temperatures to over a foot of new snow, the weather sure has changed quickly over the past week. A cooler and wetter weather pattern has taken shape over our region since Friday the 13th. As of Monday (16th) afternoon, some mountain locations have picked up 6-12 inches of new snow along with southerly winds gusting 20-30 MPH.
Wind Slabs
• Wind slabs could become reactive this week with over a foot of new snow and gusty winds. Wind slabs will be most sensitive just below ridgelines.
• Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices.
• Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
• Strong winds and local terrain features can alter the prevailing wind direction. Pay attention to cross-loading and wind-loading on unsuspecting slopes.
Early Season Conditions
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.
Check Your Winter Gear

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
Continuing Education
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with the winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
Observations
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes are still thin and lack a slab, so avalanche danger is LOW. You should be able to steer around isolated pockets of firmer wind-drifted snow, especially in steep terrain.
